meaning: First son of Adam and Eve

phonemes.desc: Voiceless uvular plosive [q] — Hebrew qof — followed by short [a], the patah under ק.
Palatal approximant [j], the yod as consonant, plus long [iː] from the hireq-yod combination, ending in alveolar nasal [n].

pronunciation.approximation: 'kah-YEEN' — the first consonant is a deep 'k' made at the back of the throat (like Arabic qāf); the second syllable is a long 'yeen'.

kin.label: Hebrew root
kin.form: q-n-h, 'to acquire, create' — the name is punned in Genesis 4:1 ('I have acquired a man')

kin.label: Ugaritic
kin.form: qyn, possibly 'smith, metalworker' (attested in Ugaritic texts)

kin.label: Aramaic
kin.form: קַיִן (Qayin), as in the Targumim and Jewish Aramaic

kin.label: Arabic
kin.form: Qābīl (قَابِيل), the Qur'anic figure corresponding to Cain

pronunciation.note: BHS points the name קַיִן (Genesis 4:1). The first vowel is a short patah [a] in the Masoretic pointing, although the qāṭīl-pattern form historically had a long *ā (reflected in the PUNICODEX macron convention Qāyīn); the second vowel is a long hireq-yod [iː]. The qof is a uvular [q], distinct from kaf. HALOT s.v. קַיִן; TDOT s.v. Cain.

domains.title: The First Murderer
domains.subtitle: Tiller, Outcast, Marked Man
domains.lead: Qāyīn is the first child of the first couple and the first human to shatter the world he was born into. A tiller of soil, he brings the fruit of his labor to God and sees it rejected while his brother's offering is accepted. The rejection does not merely disappoint him; it unlocks something ancient and violent. His story is the Bible's first meditation on envy, anger, and the blood that cries out from the ground.

cards.name: Tiller of the Ground
cards.desc: Cain works the soil, the oldest human vocation; his offering is the fruit of the earth he has labored over (Genesis 4:2–3).

cards.name: The Rejected Offering
cards.desc: God looks with favor on Abel's offering but not on Cain's; the text never explains why, leaving the reader with the mystery of divine preference (Genesis 4:4–5).

cards.name: The Mark of Cain
cards.desc: After the murder, God places a sign on Cain to protect him from vengeance, transforming the killer into a wandering, guarded man (Genesis 4:15).

cards.name: Builder of the First City
cards.desc: Cain names his city Enoch after his son, becoming the biblical ancestor of tent-dwellers, musicians, and metalworkers (Genesis 4:17–22).

symbols.name: Plowshare
symbols.meaning: His identity as a worker of the soil, later ironically turned to violence

symbols.name: Blood
symbols.meaning: The blood of Abel that cries out from the ground and cannot be silenced

symbols.name: The mark
symbols.meaning: A protective sign whose exact nature is never described; later imagined as a horn, a letter, or a visible stigma

symbols.name: City walls
symbols.meaning: Enoch, the first city, built by an outcast as a refuge against the world he has wounded

symbols.name: Bronze and iron tools
symbols.meaning: Through his descendants Tubal-cain and others, Cain becomes associated with the crafts of metalwork

mythology.lead: Qāyīn's mythology is short, dense, and endlessly reinterpreted. In a few verses, Genesis gives us the first birth, the first vocation, the first sacrifice, the first rejection, the first murder, the first lie, the first curse, and the first city.

myths.title: Two Brothers, Two Offerings
myths.text: In Eve's cry — 'I have acquired a man with the help of the LORD' (Genesis 4:1) — the Hebrew qaniti, 'I have acquired,' rings on the name Qāyīn itself; the mother already hears what the son will become. Abel (Hevel) means 'breath' or 'vapor,' and the text treats him like one: he appears only to be slain. The brothers bring parallel offerings — fruit of the ground, firstlings of the flock — 'and the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering, but for Cain and his offering he had no regard.' No reason is given, and the silence is the story's engine: later readers supplied motives by the shelf-full, but the text refuses, and the refusal is honest — favor, like weather, is not always legible. What matters is what Cain does with the unexplained. God meets him before the fall: 'Why are you angry? ... sin is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.' The first temptation scene in scripture is a warning delivered in the second person singular — God speaks to the murderer before the murder, and the chapter's whole weight hangs on that one unsent sentence.

myths.title: The First Murder
myths.text: Cain speaks to Abel — the text gives no content to the conversation, and later tradition filled the gap with a quarrel over land or over a twin sister (the Book of Jubilees 4 makes the brothers twins born with sisters, and their rivalry the world's first inheritance dispute) — and then, when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother and killed him. No weapon is named, no blow described: the Bible's first human death gets less narrative attention than any animal sacrifice in the chapter. Then God asks the question that has not stopped being asked: 'Where is Abel your brother?' And Cain answers with the first lie spoken to God: 'I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?' The grammar of the retort is immortal — a rhetorical question used as a wall, an appeal to the absurdity of responsibility, the oldest evasion on record. Every ethics since is a footnote to that unanswered question; the murderer's deflection became the syllabus of civilization, and the field where it happened has never been located because it is everywhere.

myths.title: The Curse and the Mark
myths.text: 'What have you done? Listen — your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground!' (Genesis 4:10). The earth, which Cain worked, has become a witness that cannot be silenced, and God pronounces the sentence from the same soil: now cursed from the ground that received the blood, it will no longer yield to Cain its strength; he will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth. Cain's protest is the first recorded plea against a disproportionate punishment: 'My punishment is greater than I can bear; whoever meets me will kill me.' And here the story performs its most startling act of mercy — God sets a sign (ʾôt) on Cain, not as a stigma but as a shield: 'Not so! Whoever kills Cain will suffer a vengeance sevenfold.' The mark protects the killer from the very cycle he started. Exiled east of Eden to the land of Nod — 'Wandering' — he walks out under guard. Justice and mercy are braided from the very first crime: the God who curses the murderer still stands between him and the mob, and the mark of Cain was a shelter long before it was a scar.

myths.title: The Line of Cain
myths.text: Exiled to Wandering, Cain does the most characteristically human thing in the chapter: he builds. His son is named Enoch, and the first city in the Bible is named for the boy — a wall against the world, built by the man the world could not keep. And in that city, culture explodes from his line: Jabal, father of tent-dwellers and cattle-herders; Jubal, father of the lyre and the pipe; Tubal-cain, 'forger of every bronze and iron tool.' Music, architecture, and metallurgy are all Cainite inventions — civilization born in the murderer's household. The line closes with Lamech's terrible song to his two wives: 'I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me; if Cain is avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy-sevenfold.' The arithmetic of vengeance has learned to compound. The Bible places the concert and the sword in one family tree: every city, every instrument, every blade descends from the man the ground itself testified against — and the story leaves us holding both facts at once, unable to set either down.

lore.syncretism: The Qur'an tells the story of Qābīl and Hābīl (Surah 5:27–31), offering a more explicit motive — Cain threatens to kill Abel because God accepts only Abel's sacrifice — and making Abel the first prophet-martyr; a raven shows Cain how to bury the dead. Gnostic traditions, especially the Cainites, reversed the biblical valuation and celebrated Cain as the one who resisted the creator god. Medieval Jewish legend filled in the silences of Genesis: Cain grew a horn, the mark was a letter of the divine name, and he was eventually killed by the blind Lamech, whom his own son led to mistake him for an animal. John Milton gave him a fallen grandeur in Paradise Lost, while Lord Byron made him a Romantic rebel against an unjust heaven. Across cultures, Cain is the figure who forces us to ask why violence begins and how it can be stopped.
lore.culturalLegacy: Qāyīn and his brother have become the archetype of fratricide — every killing of brother by brother carries their names. The 'mark of Cain' has been misunderstood as a sign of racial blackness and used to justify slavery and racism, though the text gives no hint of ethnicity. In literature, Cain appears as the first rebel, the first exile, the first city-builder, and the first artist of violence. Psychologically, the 'Cain complex' names the rivalry between siblings that can turn deadly. The story's central question — 'Am I my brother's keeper?' — remains a test for every society.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Qāyīn is the first human being who does not know what to do with failure. His offering is rejected, and instead of asking why or changing, he destroys the one whose offering was accepted. In that, he is the ancestor of every envious heart that mistakes another's success for its own diminishment.

The ground that receives Abel's blood becomes a witness; it will not be silent. Cain is cursed from it because the earth has absorbed what should have lived. To meditate on Cain is to meditate on the moment before violence — the warning that sin is crouching at the door — and on how rarely we heed it. The story does not let us write him off as a monster; it shows us a farmer, a brother, a city-builder, a man who could have mastered the crouching thing and did not.
lore.archaeology: No archaeological evidence links to the individual Cain, whose story belongs to the primeval history of Genesis rather than to datable history. The narrative does reflect the broader transition to agricultural and pastoral lifeways in the ancient Levant during the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods. Early settled communities, metallurgy, and the tension between farmers and herders are all part of the material backdrop against which the story was told.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Hebrew name is written קַיִן: the qof represents a voiceless uvular plosive [q], distinct from ordinary k; the patah under the qof is short, though scholars reconstruct an original long *ā in the qāṭīl-pattern form; and the yod with hireq gives the long [iː]. PUNICODEX renders the name as Qāyīn, using a macron on ā to mark the historically long vowel and a macron on ī for the hireq-yod. The q is kept plain because there is no registrable Unicode qof, but the pronunciation note preserves its uvular character. This is a Tier-1 restoration that retains a distinctive Semitic consonant and vowel length — the macrons on ā and ī are distinctive diacritics the ASCII form loses.
